subtype: Approach: rehearsing a calm firm reply [Thinking]
passage: Vishal waited until his sister left for the well, then stood in front of the small mirror in the kitchen. "Stop it," he said. Too squeaky. He tried again, lower and slower: "Stop it." Then he turned and took three steps, as if leaving the school gate. He pictured Ritu laughing, maybe copying his voice. "Then I keep walking," he whispered. "Laughing is only noise." He did it ten times, until the words came out steady and his hands stopped shaking. Next morning at the hand pump Ritu began the usual jokes. Vishal's voice was thin, but it held, and he walked away without looking back.

qa.q: Where did Vishal practise saying "Stop it"?
qa.a: He practised in front of the small mirror in the kitchen.

qa.q: Why did Vishal picture Ritu laughing before it happened?
qa.a: He was nervous and wanted to feel steady, so he imagined the laugh and decided in advance that it was only noise.

qa.q: What could Vishal add to his plan if Ritu keeps teasing after he walks away?
qa.a: He could tell a teacher what was said and when, because a calm reply may not be enough by itself and an adult can step in.

qa.q: How might a steady "Stop it" feel to Ritu compared with a squeaky one?
qa.a: A steady voice gives Ritu less to laugh at, so Ritu may lose interest, while a shaky voice could feel like a reward for teasing.

grounding: A boy rehearses a calm firm reply and walking away, imagining the bully's reaction so he is steadier.
